The reproductive strategy of the Coastrange sculpin (Cottus aleuticus) initiates with surprisingly diminutive offspring, as the wet weight at birth is a mere 0.0023 grams [Wwb = 0.0023 grams]. This minimal starting mass reflects the modest size of the eggs, which produce lecithotrophic larvae reliant on their yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. Following the exotrophic transition, juveniles experience an accelerated growth phase that ultimately leads to the attainment of an adult body mass. For males, the maximum recorded body mass in adults has been documented at 50.3 grams [Wwi = 50.3 grams], a value that stands in stark contrast to the initial size of the newly emerged alevin and underscores the substantial somatic investment required to reach the adult stage.

Sexual maturation in female Coastrange sculpin is reached at a relatively modest body length compared to the maximum sizes observed in males. Young-of-year females typically undergo the transition to puberty once they achieve a total length of approximately 4.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 4.5 centimeters]. At this milestone, the corresponding wet weight at puberty for females is approximately 0.78 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.78 grams], reflecting the physiological transition from somatic growth toward the initiation of vitellogenesis and gonadal development. This size at first gametogenesis is notably smaller than the ultimate length achieved by mature males, indicating a clear divergence in life-history trajectories between the sexes, a pattern common among many cottid fishes inhabiting cool, coastal streams.

Male Coastrange sculpin exhibit a substantially larger maximum size, with the ultimate total length for males recorded at 17 centimeters [Li = 17 centimeters], a size that enhances their ability to defend nesting territories under cobbles in fast-flowing streams. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in length likely relates to male reproductive success, as larger males are better able to defend nesting territories and attract females during the spawning period. The age at which this terminal size is achieved is closely tied to the thermal conditions of their environment. For instance, the maximum lifespan of this species, estimated at approximately 2920 days [am = approximately 2920 days] when maintained at a consistent water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], provides a prolonged window for iterative growth and reproductive output across multiple breeding seasons in these cool, productive habitats.

Comparative studies with congeneric species reveal that Cottus aleuticus exhibits a moderately paced life history relative to other members of the family Cottidae. The minimal wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0023 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0023 grams] results in larvae that must immediately commence feeding on small benthic invertebrates to fuel their rapid growth trajectory. This contrasts with the relatively substantial wet weight at puberty for females, which, at approximately 0.78 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.78 grams], necessitates several months of active feeding on benthic macroinvertebrates to accumulate sufficient lipid stores for the first spawning event. The availability of prey in the gravel-bottomed riffles they inhabit thus acts as a primary ecological driver of maturation timing.

The maximum recorded longevity of approximately 2920 days [am = approximately 2920 days] under the cool thermal conditions of 7 °C [T = 7 °C] classifies Cottus aleuticus as a relatively long-lived cottid, enabling repeated spawning events across multiple years. This extended lifespan, combined with the ultimate wet weight for males of 50.3 grams [Wwi = 50.3 grams], suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes iteroparity over semelparity, allowing males to achieve the large body sizes necessary for successful nest defense and territory acquisition in competitive breeding environments. The ultimate total length for males reaches 17 centimeters [Li = 17 centimeters], representing the endpoint of a prolonged growth trajectory that supports both physical dominance and the energetic capacity for repeated annual spawning bouts under the stable, cold conditions of Pacific Northwest coastal streams.
